theory.title: Understanding Test Cases and Sequential Execution
theory.content:
\n\n
\n\n

You wake up in the damaged ship. MENTOR-9's voice crackles through damaged speakers.

"PROTO-7, can you hear me? Your voice synthesizer is offline, but you can communicate through diagnostic protocols—Robot Framework test outputs."

What is a Test Case?

In Robot Framework, a test case is a named sequence of actions (keywords) that verify behavior. Think of it like a checklist:

  • Each test case has a name
  • Below the name, you write the steps (keywords) to execute
  • Keywords execute sequentially from top to bottom
  • If all steps succeed, the test passes ✅
  • If any step fails, the test fails ❌

The Basic Structure

Every Robot Framework file has sections marked by ***. Here's your first test:

*** Test Cases ***
My Test Name
    Log    First action
    Log    Second action
    Log    Third action

⚠️ Critical Spacing Rules

  • Test names start at the left margin (no indentation)
  • Keywords must be indented with at least 2 spaces (4 spaces recommended for readability)
  • Separate keywords and arguments with at least 2 spaces (4 is standard)
  • Tabs can work but may cause issues with mixed editors—stick to spaces

Best practice: Use 4 spaces consistently throughout your test files!

Why 4 Spaces?

Robot Framework's minimum requirements:

  • Test case body: Minimum 2 spaces indentation
  • Keyword/argument separation: Minimum 2 spaces

Valid examples (all work):

*** Test Cases ***
Test With 2 Spaces
  Log  Message

Test With 4 Spaces
    Log    Message

Test With 6 Spaces
      Log      Message

Why 4 spaces is the standard:

  • Better readability and visual hierarchy
  • Consistent across teams and projects
  • Matches Python's PEP 8 style guide
  • Clearly distinguishes test body from test name
  • Avoids tab/space mixing issues

The Log Keyword

The Log keyword outputs messages to the test log file (log.html). It's your primary debugging and communication tool.

Syntax:

Log    Your message here

Why Use Log?

  • Debugging: See what values variables have
  • Verification: Confirm code paths execute
  • Documentation: Add runtime notes to reports
  • Progress tracking: Show test execution stages

Sequential Execution

When you write multiple Log keywords:

  1. Robot Framework executes the first Log
  2. Then the second Log
  3. Then the third Log, etc.
  4. Order matters! They execute top to bottom.

This makes tests read like documentation—anyone can understand the workflow by reading from top to bottom.

MENTOR-9 nods. "Your turn, PROTO-7. Create a test case called 'Boot Sequence' with 5 sequential log messages showing your systems coming online. Show me you can communicate a multi-stage process."

exercises.title: System Diagnostics with Severity
exercises.description: Use log levels to indicate message severity and prioritize issues.

story.setup: MENTOR-9: "Good, but you're sending everything at the same priority. Not all messages are equal—learn to indicate severity. Some systems are fine, some have warnings, some are critical."
story.context: The ship has multiple system states. Log levels help prioritize what to fix first. INFO for normal status, WARN for potential issues, ERROR for critical problems.
story.success: MENTOR-9: "Perfect! Now I can see at a glance: navigation is stable (INFO), hull has minor damage (WARN), and life support needs urgent attention (ERROR). Severity indicators save lives."

instructions: Create a test case named 'System Status Report'
Log 6 different ship systems with appropriate severity levels:
- 'Hull breach detected in sector 7' at WARN level
- 'Sensor array: Degraded performance' at WARN level
- 'Life support: Critical failure imminent' at ERROR level
- 'Communication array: Total failure' at ERROR level
hints: Syntax for log levels: Log    message    LEVEL
Valid levels: INFO, WARN, ERROR (uppercase)
INFO is the default if no level is specified
The level comes AFTER the message, separated by spaces
Use INFO for normal status, WARN for concerns, ERROR for critical issues
You should have 2 INFO, 2 WARN, and 2 ERROR messages
exercises.solution:
*** Test Cases ***
System Status Report
    Log    Navigation system: Operational    INFO
    Log    Power core: Stable    INFO
    Log    Hull breach detected in sector 7    WARN
    Log    Sensor array: Degraded performance    WARN
    Log    Life support: Critical failure imminent    ERROR
    Log    Communication array: Total failure    ERROR

theory.title: Log Levels and Message Severity
theory.content:
\n\n
\n\n

MENTOR-9 pulls up the ship's log display. It's cluttered with hundreds of messages—all appearing equally important.

"This is chaos, PROTO-7. We need to prioritize. That's where log levels come in."

What Are Log Levels?

Log levels indicate the severity or importance of a message. Robot Framework supports several levels:

LevelUsageExample
INFONormal operational messages"User logged in successfully"
WARNPotential issues, non-critical"API response slow (3.2s)"
ERRORErrors that don't stop the test"Database connection timeout"
DEBUGDetailed debugging info"Variable value: x = 42"
TRACEVery detailed debugging"Entering loop iteration 5"

Syntax

Log    Normal message
Log    Normal message    INFO
Log    Warning message    WARN
Log    Error occurred    ERROR

Notes:

  • First line: No level specified = INFO by default
  • Second line: INFO explicitly stated (same as first)
  • Third line: WARN level for warnings
  • Fourth line: ERROR level for errors

When to Use Each Level

  • INFO: Standard progress updates ("Starting test", "Page loaded", "System operational")
  • WARN: Things that aren't quite right but test continues ("Slow response", "Deprecated API", "Minor damage")
  • ERROR: Problems that might cause failures ("Connection failed", "Critical system offline", "Data corruption")
  • DEBUG: Development details ("Variable x = ${x}", "Entering function")
  • TRACE: Very verbose debugging (usually not needed)

Visual Impact in Reports

In the HTML log report:

  • INFO messages appear in black
  • WARN messages appear in orange
  • ERROR messages appear in red

This makes critical issues immediately visible when reviewing test results!

Real-World Example

*** Test Cases ***
API Health Check
    Log    Starting health check...    INFO
    Log    Database: Connected    INFO
    Log    API response time: 2.1s (slow)    WARN
    Log    Cache server: Unreachable    ERROR
    Log    Health check complete    INFO

Reading this log, you immediately know:

  • ✅ Database is fine (INFO)
  • ⚠️ API is slow but working (WARN)
  • ❌ Cache server is down (ERROR) - investigate this first!

MENTOR-9: "Analyze our ship systems. Report on 6 different systems using appropriate log levels. Show me you can communicate priority—what's working, what's concerning, what's critical."

exercises.title: Dual Channel Communication

story.success: MENTOR-9: "Perfect! I saw your progress updates in real-time on console, and now I'm reviewing the detailed diagnostic log. You understand the dual-channel paradigm. This is how we monitor long-running operations."

Use Log To Console for these progress updates:
Use Log for these detailed records:

Log writes to log.html (detailed permanent record)

Use Log for detailed information you want in the report
Syntax is the same: keyword    message

Mix them appropriately: console for progress, log for details

theory.title: Log vs Log To Console: When to Use Each
theory.content:
\n\n
\n\n

MENTOR-9 taps a display. "PROTO-7, notice how you only see Log messages after opening the HTML report? Sometimes you need real-time feedback while tests run. That's where Log To Console comes in."

Two Output Destinations

Robot Framework has two main logging keywords:

KeywordOutputWhen VisibleUse Case
Log log.html report After test completes Permanent record, detailed debugging
Log To Console Terminal/console Immediately, during execution Real-time feedback, progress tracking

Example: Progress Tracking

*** Test Cases ***
Long Running Test
    Log To Console    Starting test suite...
    Log               Detailed step 1: Initializing database connection
    Log To Console    Progress: 25% complete
    Log               Detailed step 2: Loading test data (1000 records)
    Log To Console    Progress: 50% complete
    Log               Detailed step 3: Running validation queries
    Log To Console    Progress: 75% complete
    Log               Detailed step 4: Cleanup and verification
    Log To Console    Test complete - 100%

When to Use Log

  • Recording variable values for later analysis
  • Detailed debugging information
  • Creating an audit trail of test actions
  • Anything you want preserved in the HTML report
  • Information that's too verbose for console

When to Use Log To Console

  • Progress updates for long-running tests
  • Quick checks during test development
  • CI/CD pipeline output (visible in build logs)
  • Immediate feedback without opening HTML reports
  • Percentage completion indicators
  • High-level status messages

Pro Tip: Use Both Together!

It's common and recommended to use both in the same test. This gives you:

  • Real-time progress in the console (what's happening now)
  • Detailed records in the HTML report (what happened and why)

Real-World API Test Example

*** Test Cases ***
API Load Test
    Log To Console    Starting API load test with 100 requests...
    Log               Request URL: https://api.example.com/users
    Log               Headers: Content-Type=application/json
    
    FOR    ${i}    IN RANGE    100
        ${response}    GET    /users/${i}
        Log            Response ${i}: Status=${response.status}, Time=${response.elapsed}
        Log To Console    Completed: ${i}/100 requests
    END
    
    Log To Console    Load test complete!
    Log               Total time: 45.2 seconds, Average response: 452ms

In this example:

  • Console shows: "Starting...", "1/100", "2/100", ... "100/100", "Complete!"
  • Log file shows: URL, headers, every individual response with timing data

You get immediate progress feedback AND detailed records for debugging!

MENTOR-9: "Run an extended diagnostic. Use Log To Console for progress updates (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) so I can monitor in real-time. Use Log for detailed technical findings that I'll review in the report later."

exercises.title: Syntax Flexibility - The Language's True Nature
exercises.description: Discover Robot Framework's permissive syntax: case insensitivity and spacing variations.

story.setup: MENTOR-9: "PROTO-7, I need to teach you something most training programs hide. Robot Framework is more flexible than you think. It's not as strict as other languages."
story.context: Robot Framework's parser is designed to be forgiving. Keywords are case-insensitive, and spacing has flexibility. Understanding what's ALLOWED helps you recognize different coding styles in the wild.
story.success: MENTOR-9: "See? They all work! Robot Framework is forgiving. Now you understand: the language is permissive, but teams standardize for readability. You've learned what's POSSIBLE. Later, you'll learn what's PREFERRED."

instructions: Create a test case named 'Syntax Flexibility Test'
Demonstrate case insensitivity by using Log in different cases:
- Use 'LoG' (mixed case) to output 'Mixed case works'
- Use 'Log To Console' (standard spacing) to output 'Standard spacing'
- Use 'Log  To  Console' (double spaces) to output 'Extra spaces work'
- Use 'LogToConsole' (no spaces) to output 'No spaces work too'
hints: Keywords are case-insensitive: Log = log = LOG = LoG
Multi-word keywords can have varying spaces: 'Log To Console' = 'Log  To  Console' = 'LogToConsole'
This is a FEATURE of Robot Framework, not a bug
Best practice: use standard capitalization (Log, Log To Console)
But when reading others' code, you'll see variations
All variations produce identical results
exercises.solution:
*** Test Cases ***
Syntax Flexibility Test
    Log    Standard capitalization
    log    Lowercase works too
    LOG    Uppercase works
    LoG    Mixed case works
    Log To Console    Standard spacing
    Log  To  Console    Extra spaces work
    LogToConsole    No spaces work too

theory.title: Robot Framework's Syntax Flexibility
theory.content:
\n\n
\n\n

MENTOR-9's optics dim thoughtfully. "PROTO-7, before we go further, you need to understand something fundamental about Robot Framework's design philosophy."

"It was built to be readable by humans, not just parseable by machines. That means it's surprisingly forgiving."

Case Insensitivity

In Robot Framework, keywords are case-insensitive. All of these are identical:

Log    Message
log    Message
LOG    Message
LoG    Message
l O g    Message

They all execute the same keyword! Robot Framework converts keywords to a normalized form internally.

Why This Matters

  • You'll encounter different styles in different codebases
  • Some teams prefer Log, others prefer log
  • Both are valid—it's a style choice, not a syntax requirement
  • Understanding this prevents confusion when reading others' code

Spacing Flexibility in Multi-Word Keywords

Keywords with multiple words (like Log To Console) also have spacing flexibility:

Log To Console    Message
Log  To  Console    Message
LogToConsole    Message
log to console    Message
LOGTOCONSOLE    Message

All of these work! Robot Framework normalizes spacing and case.

What's Standard vs What's Allowed

FeatureWhat's AllowedWhat's Recommended
Keyword case Any case: Log, log, LOG, LoG Title Case: Log, Should Be Equal
Keyword spacing Any spacing: LogToConsole, Log To Console Single spaces: Log To Console
Indentation Minimum 2 spaces, any even amount 4 spaces consistently
Argument separation Minimum 2 spaces, tabs, or more 4 spaces consistently

Why Standards Exist

Robot Framework allows flexibility, but teams standardize for:

  • Readability: Consistent style is easier to scan
  • Maintainability: Code reviews are simpler with one style
  • Diff clarity: Version control shows real changes, not style changes
  • Team collaboration: Everyone writes in the same style

The Design Philosophy

Robot Framework was designed to be keyword-driven and readable. The creators chose flexibility to:

  • Reduce syntax errors (case typos don't break tests)
  • Allow natural language-like test writing
  • Focus on WHAT you're testing, not HOW you capitalize
  • Make tests accessible to non-programmers

Variable Names Are ALSO Flexible!

Just like keywords, variable names are also case-insensitive and spacing-flexible:

${myVar}    # Same as...
${MyVar}    # ...and same as...
${MYVAR}    # ...and same as...
${my_var}   # ...and same as...
${m y v a r} # ...these are all THE SAME variable!

Robot Framework normalizes variable names just like it normalizes keywords. This means:

  • ✅ Keywords: Case-insensitive and spacing-flexible (Log = log = LOG)
  • ✅ Variables: Case-insensitive and spacing-flexible (${x} = ${X} = ${x_})
  • ✅ Everything is flexible! Robot Framework prioritizes readability over strict syntax

MENTOR-9: "Now demonstrate your understanding. Write a test using multiple keyword case variations and spacing styles. Show me they all work. Then you'll truly understand Robot Framework's flexibility."

exercises.title: Section Headers - The Framework's Structure

theory.title: Robot Framework File Structure: All Sections
theory.content:
\n\n
\n\n

MENTOR-9 projects a hologram of a Robot Framework file, divided into glowing sections.

"You've been writing tests in isolation. But real RF files are organized. They have multiple sections, each with a specific purpose."

The Main Sections

SectionPurposeWhat Goes Here
*** Settings *** Configuration Documentation, library imports, setup/teardown, tags, timeouts
*** Variables *** Data definitions ${scalar}, @{list}, &{dict} variable definitions
*** Test Cases *** Your tests All test cases with their keywords
*** Keywords *** Reusable functions Custom keywords you create for reuse across tests
*** Comments *** File comments Multi-line comments ignored by RF (rarely used)

Note: The four sections you'll use 99% of the time are Settings, Variables, Test Cases, and Keywords. The *** Comments *** section exists but is rarely used (single-line comments with # are more common).

Complete File Example

*** Settings ***
Documentation    Ship diagnostic test suite
Library          Collections

*** Variables ***
${SHIP_NAME}     Starlight Explorer
@{SYSTEMS}       Navigation  Power  Life Support

*** Test Cases ***
System Check
    Log    Checking ${SHIP_NAME} systems
    Check All Systems

*** Keywords ***
Check All Systems
    FOR    ${system}    IN    @{SYSTEMS}
        Log    Checking ${system}...
    END

Section Details

1. Settings Section

Configuration and imports. Common settings:

  • Documentation: Describes the test suite
  • Library: Import external libraries (Collections, String, etc.)
  • Suite Setup/Teardown: Run keywords before/after all tests
  • Test Setup/Teardown: Run keywords before/after each test
  • Force Tags: Apply tags to all tests
  • Test Timeout: Maximum time for tests
2. Variables Section

Define variables used throughout the file:

  • ${scalar}: Single values (strings, numbers)
  • @{list}: Lists of items
  • &{dict}: Key-value pairs (dictionaries)
3. Test Cases Section

Your actual tests. You've been using this section already!

4. Keywords Section

Custom keywords you create. Like functions in programming—reusable blocks of actions.

Section Header Formatting

Like keywords, section headers have spacing flexibility:

*** Settings ***     # Standard (3 spaces inside)
***Settings***       # No spaces (valid)
*** Settings***      # Left space only (valid)
***Settings ***      # Right space only (valid)
***  Settings  ***   # Multiple spaces (valid)

All are valid! But the standard is *** Section *** with 1 space on each side.

Section Order Conventions

While not enforced, the standard order is:

  1. Settings (configuration comes first)
  2. Variables (define data before using it)
  3. Test Cases (the main content)
  4. Keywords (helper functions at the end)

This is convention, not requirement. RF will parse sections in any order. But following conventions makes code predictable.

Optional Sections

You don't need all four sections in every file:

  • A file with just *** Test Cases *** is valid
  • You can skip Settings, Variables, or Keywords if not needed
  • But *** Test Cases *** is required (otherwise, what are you testing?)

Real-World Structure

*** Settings ***
Documentation    User authentication tests
Library          SeleniumLibrary
Suite Setup      Open Browser    ${URL}    chrome
Suite Teardown   Close All Browsers

*** Variables ***
${URL}           https://example.com
${USERNAME}      testuser@example.com
${PASSWORD}      SecurePass123

*** Test Cases ***
Successful Login
    Enter Credentials    ${USERNAME}    ${PASSWORD}
    Click Login Button
    Verify Dashboard Loaded

Invalid Password
    Enter Credentials    ${USERNAME}    WrongPassword
    Click Login Button
    Verify Error Message    Invalid credentials

*** Keywords ***
Enter Credentials
    [Arguments]    ${user}    ${pass}
    Input Text     id=username    ${user}
    Input Text     id=password    ${pass}

Click Login Button
    Click Button    id=login

Verify Dashboard Loaded
    Wait Until Page Contains    Welcome

This shows a complete, realistic test file with all sections working together.

MENTOR-9: "Create a file with all four sections. Add documentation, define variables, write a test, and create a custom keyword. Show me you understand the complete structure."
